description: Hand-written source for the Engineering Encyclopedia: concept entries that the catalogue does not hold (definitions, synonyms, abbreviations, shop terms, relations between concepts) and the calculators each concept is calculated with. Calculator identities, names, labs, categories, tiers and aliases come from catalog/gearhead-catalog.json and the engine, never from here. catalog/build-encyclopedia.js joins the two into catalog/gearhead-encyclopedia.json; catalog/check-encyclopedia.js validates both.

provenance_default.note: Definitions in this file were drafted for the Issue #23 proof of concept (2026-10-26) and source-checked the same day. review_status: draft-unreviewed = no source verified; citation-partial = some claims supported by the cited sources, the rest listed in review_notes; citation-verified = every claim checked against the cited sources by Claude (not owner-approved); reviewed = approved by a named reviewer on a date (owner only). Every source was fetched and read for the claim in its "supports" field. Do not set reviewed without a named reviewer and date.

relation_types.broader: the target is the more general concept (this entry is a kind or part of it)
relation_types.narrower: the target is a more specific concept
relation_types.prerequisite: the target must be known or calculated first
relation_types.not-equivalent: often confused with this entry but NOT the same quantity; a note saying why is required

ambiguous.note: Shop shorthand for a compression ratio. It usually means the static (mechanical) ratio, but the dynamic and crankcase ratios are different quantities.
Without a qualifier it usually means the static ratio; the dynamic ratio (from the intake valve closing point) and a two-stroke crankcase ratio are different quantities.
Used for a suspension spring and for a valve spring; the calculators are different.

concepts.definition: The ratio of the total cylinder volume with the piston at bottom dead centre to the compressed volume with it at top dead centre: (swept volume + clearance volume) ÷ clearance volume. The clearance volume is the combustion chamber, head gasket, deck clearance and piston volume added together; a domed piston reduces it, while a dish or valve reliefs add to it.
concepts.distinctions: It is fixed by geometry. It is not the pressure measured on a compression gauge, and it is not the dynamic ratio, which starts compression only when the intake valve closes.

related.note: The dynamic ratio uses only the stroke left after the intake valve closes, so it is always lower.
Cranking compression is a measured pressure (psi or bar), not a volume ratio.

sources.title: How To Calculate Engine Compression Ratio And Displacement
sources.author: Robert Poole
sources.supports: The volume ratio and its four components. A dome is "expressed as a negative volume"; a dish or valve reliefs are "expressed as a positive".

boost_cr.note: Takes static CR as an input.

head_gasket_vol.note: Computes one of the clearance-volume components.

concepts.definition: The compression ratio counted from the moment the intake valve closes, using the piston position at intake valve closing instead of bottom dead centre.
concepts.distinctions: It depends on the camshaft (intake valve closing point) and rod length as well as the static geometry.

related.note: The static ratio uses the full stroke; the dynamic ratio only the part after the intake valve closes.

sources.title: Compression ratio calculator: what compression ratio actually means
sources.supports: Dynamic CR depends on cam timing, specifically the intake valve closing event.

concepts.review_notes: Source ties dynamic CR to intake valve closing but gives no formula. Not yet verified: the exact calculation (piston position at IVC) and the role of rod length. Only forum material was found for those; a manufacturer or textbook source is still needed.

concepts.definition: In a crankcase-scavenged two-stroke engine, the ratio of the crankcase volume with the piston at top dead centre to the volume with it at bottom dead centre.
concepts.distinctions: It describes the crankcase pumping that transfers the charge, not compression in the combustion chamber.

related.note: Measured in the crankcase of a two-stroke, not in the cylinder.

concepts.review_notes: No authoritative source found in this check (searches returned forums only). Needs a two-stroke reference (for example a two-stroke design text) before it can be cited.

concepts.definition: The crankshaft angle, usually given in degrees after bottom dead centre, at which the intake valve closes. Closing it later lets the rising piston push some of the charge back into the intake at low engine speed, lowering cylinder pressure and low-speed torque; at high engine speed the moving air column keeps filling the cylinder, which is why high-rpm engines use a later closing.
concepts.distinctions: Cam cards give it at a stated lift (advertised or 0.050 in); figures at different lift references are not interchangeable. The card values also assume the cam is installed as intended: retarding the cam delays intake closing and advancing moves the intake event earlier, which is why cams are degreed to check the events.

sources.title: Valve Timing Events And The Order Of Importance
sources.author: Rick Kertes
sources.warning: Author and dates confirmed only through Muck Rack's author listing (https://muckrack.com/rick-kertes/articles); neither article page displays a byline or date. Also printed by Engine Builder, 15 Apr 2016 (https://www.enginebuildermag.com/?p=16181).
sources.supports: "If the valve is closed late, the air charge will flow back into the intake manifold"; late closing "limits low-end power"; "High RPM race engines benefit immensely from a continuation of airflow."

sources.title: Camshaft Tech 101
sources.author: Michael Ferrara
sources.supports: "the piston may pump some of the intake charge out of the cylinder."

sources.title: Demystifying the Camshaft: Part 1 – Valve Events
sources.author: Colin Holte
sources.supports: Low-speed reversion and high-rpm charge momentum.

sources.title: Effect Of Changes In Cam Timing And Lobe Separation Angle
sources.supports: Retarding "Delays Intake Closing Event"; advancing "Begins Intake Event Sooner".

sources.title: Back To Basics: Understanding A Cam Card With Erson Cams
sources.author: Jeff Smith
sources.supports: The lift references, and repositioning a cam whose degreed events are out.

cam_card.note: Outputs all valve events, including IVC.

concepts.definition: The total volume swept by all the pistons in one stroke: bore area times stroke times the number of cylinders.
concepts.distinctions: It excludes the clearance (combustion chamber) volume.

sources.title: How To Calculate Engine Compression Ratio And Displacement
sources.author: Robert Poole
sources.supports: Swept volume from bore, stroke and cylinders, kept separate from compressed volume.

reverse_displacement.note: Solves the same relation for bore or stroke.

concepts.definition: Cylinder bore divided by piston stroke. At exactly 1 the engine is called square; above 1 it is oversquare, below 1 undersquare.

related.note: The rod/stroke ratio compares the connecting rod length, not the bore, with the stroke.

sources.title: How bore vs. stroke can affect horsepower
sources.author: Brandan Gillogly
sources.supports: Oversquare "is able to rev very high without extreme piston speed"; a larger bore offers "more real estate to fit larger intake and exhaust valves that flow more air".

sources.title: Stroke ratio
sources.supports: "Square" = 1:1, and oversquare as higher rpm "by lowering maximum piston speed".

concepts.distinctions: Mean piston speed is set by the stroke and the engine speed, not by the bore. As a general design tendency, oversquare engines often pair a shorter stroke with a larger bore that leaves room for larger valves. A shorter stroke means lower piston speed at a given rpm, but the bore-to-stroke ratio alone does not guarantee a higher safe rpm.
caveats: The mean-piston-speed formula sources (Mean Piston Speed entry) support "set by the stroke and the engine speed" and "lower piston speed at a given rpm".
"Does not guarantee a higher safe rpm" is a deliberate editorial limit on the claim, not a sourced statement.

concepts.definition: Connecting rod centre-to-centre length divided by the crankshaft stroke.
concepts.distinctions: A higher ratio reduces the connecting rod's angle, which lowers the side thrust of the piston skirt against the cylinder wall and keeps the piston near top dead centre slightly longer (dwell). Production engines commonly fall between about 1.4 and 1.8 or more, but the right ratio depends on the engine's purpose and rpm range rather than one universal target.

related.note: Compares rod length, not bore, with the stroke.

sources.title: Engine anatomy: rod to stroke ratio
sources.supports: Reduced angularity, lower skirt side thrust, dwell, "1.4 through to 1.8 or more", and different ratios suggested for different rpm ranges.

sources.title: How A Stroker Crankshaft Affects Piston Speed and Inertia
sources.supports: Secondary support only.

connecting_rod_angularity.note: Is the angle this ratio sets.

concepts.definition: The average speed of the piston over a crank revolution. The piston travels two strokes per revolution, so mean piston speed is twice the stroke times the engine speed. With stroke in inches and engine speed in rpm: feet per minute = stroke × 2 × rpm ÷ 12.

sources.title: IC engine lecture notes
sources.publisher: FAMU-FSU College of Engineering course web space
sources.warning: No author or date on the document.
sources.supports: The mean piston speed "Vp = 2NS", independent of rod length.

sources.title: How A Stroker Crankshaft Affects Piston Speed and Inertia
sources.supports: The shop-unit formula, "Mean Piston Speed (fpm)=(Stroke x 2 x RPM)/12", and that the true maximum needs rod length and angularity.

sources.title: Engine anatomy: rod to stroke ratio
sources.supports: Rod length changes how long the piston dwells near TDC.

concepts.distinctions: It is an average over the revolution. Connecting-rod length does not change it at a given stroke and rpm; rod length changes how the piston's instantaneous speed varies through the stroke, including where and how high its peak speed is.
caveats: No textbook (Heywood) could be accessed; the independent engineering source is an unattributed course document.

concepts.definition: The constant pressure that, acting on the pistons over each power stroke, would give the engine's measured brake (output) torque. It compares torque per unit displacement between engines of different sizes.

related.note: IMEP is the indicated (in-cylinder) value; BMEP is what remains at the crankshaft.

sources.title: Mean effective pressure
sources.supports: BMEP is calculated from measured (dynamometer) brake torque; MEP compares engines of different sizes.

concepts.definition: The mean effective pressure worked out from the cylinder pressure acting on the pistons over the complete engine cycle. Over the complete cycle it already includes the pumping work, but not mechanical friction.

related.note: BMEP is IMEP minus FMEP: friction, plus pumping when gross IMEP is used.

concepts.distinctions: Some texts quote a gross IMEP over the compression and expansion strokes only, which leaves out the pumping work; check which one a figure uses. BMEP is lower than IMEP by the friction mean effective pressure.

sources.title: Mean effective pressure
sources.supports: IMEP is calculated from in-cylinder pressure over the complete cycle, so it includes pumping work; friction is accounted for by FMEP = IMEP - BMEP.

concepts.review_notes: Revised 2026-10-26: the draft said IMEP is taken "before friction and pumping losses", which the source contradicts for IMEP over the complete cycle (net IMEP). The gross/net distinction in the "watch out" text is standard usage but was not confirmed in the fetched source.

concepts.definition: The part of the indicated mean effective pressure lost to engine friction (and, in many definitions, pumping): IMEP minus BMEP.

sources.title: Mean effective pressure
sources.supports: FMEP = IMEP - BMEP.

concepts.review_notes: Supported: FMEP = IMEP - BMEP. Not confirmed in the source: whether pumping is counted in FMEP depends on whether net or gross IMEP is used; the definition keeps that hedge.

concepts.definition: The cylinder pressure read on a compression gauge while the engine is turned by the starter.
concepts.distinctions: It is a measured pressure that depends on cranking speed, valve timing and sealing, not a geometric ratio.

sources.title: How to perform a cranking compression test
sources.supports: Measured with a compression gauge in the plug hole while the engine is cranked by the starter; cranking speed, throttle opening and number of strokes affect the reading; it tests sealing.

concepts.review_notes: Supported except "valve timing" as a factor, which the source does not mention.

concepts.definition: The gap between the two ends of a piston ring when it is installed square in the cylinder bore. It is measured with a feeler gauge with the ring pushed square into the bore below the deck, with a torque plate fitted where the engine builder uses one.

sources.title: How to measure and set proper ring end gap for your pistons
sources.supports: Every sentence, including "for every .001″ over … the ring gap increases by .00314″".

concepts.distinctions: Too tight and the ring ends can butt together, which can destroy the piston; too wide and combustion gas leaks past, costing power. Higher-boost engines use wider gaps, and the gap grows by about 3.14 times any increase in bore diameter.

concepts.definition: The last fixed gear reduction between the transmission and the driven wheels. On a typical rear-drive axle it is the ring-and-pinion ratio in the differential; on front-wheel-drive vehicles the final drive is located inside the transaxle.
concepts.distinctions: The overall ratio in a given gear is the transmission gear ratio times the final drive ratio; for example, 2.52 × 4.56 = 11.49. Some aftermarket charts call that overall figure the 'final drive', so check which number a chart means.

sources.title: Final Drives
sources.supports: "In front-wheel drive vehicles, the final drive is located inside the transaxle."

sources.title: Mechanical Power Transmission Fundamentals
sources.author: Robert P. Tata, P.E.
sources.supports: "The equation for the overall ratio of the compound gear train is the product of the two individual ratios": the general basis of the watch-out.

sources.title: What Is Rear End Gear Ratio and How Is It Calculated?
sources.author: Gearstar Performance (company byline)
sources.warning: It calls the product the "final drive ratio", which is the terminology note in the watch-out.
sources.supports: "Most automobiles use gear ratios in the drive axle and the transmission to multiply power. When you multiply the two ratios, it equals the final drive ratio." The product rule for a vehicle.

sources.title: GM Drive Ratios
sources.warning: No author; undated (page metadata modified 21 Jul 2016). The page states no formula; the product is shown by its numbers, not in words.
sources.supports: Primary data: TH350 1st gear 2.52 with a 4.56 axle listed as a "final drive" of 11.49; 4L80E 2.48 with a 5.13 axle as 12.72. Both equal gear × axle. Supports the example and the terminology note.

sources.title: Tractive Effort Curves in Gearbox Analyse
sources.author: N. Repčić, I. Šarić, V. Avdić (Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, Sarajevo)
sources.warning: Its equation did not extract, so it is not cited for the multiplication itself.
sources.supports: "Tractive effort is obtained by multiplying engine torque and the overall gear ratio (gear and final drive)": the overall ratio combines the gear and the final drive.

sources.title: Final drive ratio
sources.warning: Anonymous. Corroboration only; no claim rests on it alone.
sources.supports: Corroboration of the product rule.

sources.title: Ring and Pinion Gear Selection for Optimal Performance
sources.publisher: CarTech Books (excerpt from High Performance Axles, Differentials and Drivelines)
sources.warning: Author not named on the page.
sources.supports: The ring-and-pinion ratio.

caveats: No OEM service manual or automotive textbook passage could be opened online for the overall-ratio rule.

concepts.definition: The pair of gears in a differential: the pinion on the driveshaft input turns the ring gear on the differential carrier. The number of ring-gear teeth divided by the number of pinion teeth is the axle ratio; for example, 41 ÷ 10 = 4.10:1.

sources.title: Ring and Pinion Gear Selection for Optimal Performance
sources.publisher: CarTech Books (excerpt from High Performance Axles, Differentials and Drivelines)
sources.warning: Author not named on the page.
sources.supports: "take the number of ring gear teeth and divide by the number of pinion teeth", with the 41 ÷ 10 = 4.10 example.

sources.title: Final drive ratio
sources.warning: Anonymous. Corroboration only; no claim rests on it alone.
sources.supports: Corroboration only.

concepts.definition: The ratio of input-shaft to output-shaft speed of the transmission in a given gear.
concepts.review_notes: No source fetched that defines a transmission gear ratio as input speed / output speed. cars-data.com only uses "gearbox ratio" in the overall-ratio formula.

concepts.definition: A sun gear, planet gears on a carrier and an outer ring gear. Holding or driving different members gives different ratios; automatic transmissions are built from them.

sources.title: Epicyclic (Planetary) Gears Explained
sources.supports: Sun, planets on a carrier and ring; holding or driving different members gives different ratios; fundamental to automatic transmissions.

concepts.definition: The highest engine speed reached at full throttle with the transmission output held stationary (brake stall). It is set by the converter's internal blade geometry and the engine's torque, so the same converter stalls at a different speed behind a different engine.
concepts.distinctions: Flash stall is the speed the engine flashes to right after the brake or transbrake is released on a launch. It also depends on vehicle weight, tires and suspension, so it is hard to predict. Brake stall is more predictable, but any calculated figure is an estimate; the stall measured with the actual engine and converter is what counts.

sources.title: High Performance Converters: Stall Speed, Core Selection, and More
sources.author: Joe Allen and Andy Dumas
sources.supports: The definition, flash stall and its dependence on weight, tires and suspension, and brake stall being calculable.

torque_converter.note: Torque Converter Stall / Launch: Uses a known converter stall speed as an input to calculate launch speed and theoretical wheel torque. It does not predict or calculate stall speed. The actual stall speed must come from the converter manufacturer or a measured stall test.

caveats: "Any calculated figure is an estimate" and "the measured stall is what counts" are a more cautious editorial qualification, not a new sourced claim.

concepts.definition: A differential that limits the speed difference between the two driven wheels so torque can still reach the wheel with more grip.
concepts.distinctions: A locker is a different device (it locks the axles together); shop talk often lumps them together.

sources.title: How it Works - the 'Simple' Version (Part 1)
sources.supports: Limited-slip differentials generate internal friction to resist a speed difference and send torque to the wheel with grip.

concepts.review_notes: Not confirmed in the source: the "watch out" statement about lockers.

concepts.definition: For a limited-slip differential, the largest ratio of torque between the high-traction and low-traction wheels that it can sustain before the wheels slip relative to each other.

sources.title: Ask Torsen: Torque Bias Ratio Functional Questions
sources.warning: Date from Torsen's archive listing; the post page itself shows no date.
sources.supports: "T(high) = T(low) X TBR", "zero multiplied by 4.5 still equals zero", and brakes providing reaction torque.

concepts.distinctions: For a torque-biasing differential such as a Torsen, the high-traction wheel can receive at most the low-traction wheel's torque multiplied by the TBR. With one wheel in the air, that is zero times the TBR, which is still zero; applying the brakes lightly gives the differential reaction torque to work against.

concepts.definition: The angle between the two shafts joined by a universal joint. A single U-joint running at an angle makes the output speed rise and fall twice per revolution. On a conventional two-joint driveshaft this cancels out only when the operating angles at both ends are equal and the two inboard yokes are in line (in phase); that rule is specific to the two-joint layout and is not a rule for every driveline.

sources.title: Universal Joints catalogue P-8189-HD
sources.supports: The output "gaining, then lagging … twice in each revolution", and cancellation with equal angles and aligned inboard lugs: the kinematic principle.

sources.title: Driveshaft Tech
sources.supports: The ½° and 2° figures, centerlines parallel within ½°, and vibration that is hard to tell from imbalance: application-specific recommendations.

concepts.distinctions: The cancellation rule above is a general kinematic principle. Recommended angle limits are application-specific: for its driveshafts, Mark Williams Enterprises gives about ½° as optimal and about 2° as the most for racing, with the transmission and pinion centerlines parallel within ½°. Uneven angles cause a vibration that is easily mistaken for an out-of-balance shaft.

pinion_angle_change.note: Computes the pinion-angle change that alters the rear operating angle.

concepts.definition: The rotational speed at which a driveshaft's first bending natural frequency is excited, so it whirls and can fail.

sources.title: Driveshaft Tech
sources.supports: "Critical speed is the speed at which a spinning shaft will become unstable", and vibration is amplified when the whirling frequency matches the natural frequency.

concepts.definition: The most torque a clutch can transmit without slipping, set by clamp load, friction coefficient, mean friction radius and the number of friction surfaces.

sources.title: Fundamentals of clutches
sources.author: Temitayo Oketola
sources.supports: Torque capacity depends on friction coefficient, normal (clamp) force, number of friction surfaces and the inner and outer radii.

concepts.review_notes: The source shows the formula only as an image, which could not be read; the variables are confirmed, the exact form (mean radius) is not.

concepts.definition: The force needed to compress a suspension spring by a unit distance, measured at the spring.
concepts.distinctions: It is not the wheel rate: the rate felt at the wheel is the spring rate multiplied by the motion ratio squared, so it is lower than the spring rate whenever the motion ratio is below 1 (for example, 400 lb/in × 0.7² = 196 lb/in).

related.note: Wheel rate = spring rate × motion ratio².

sources.title: Spring rate in racing suspension: wheel rate, motion ratio and how to calculate what your tire actually feels
sources.author: Aaron Lambert
sources.supports: "the force required to compress or extend a spring by one unit of distance", and WR = k × MR² with the 196 lb/in example.

concepts.definition: The force needed to compress a valve spring by a unit distance, usually quoted in lb/in. For a spring with a constant rate, open pressure = installed (seat) pressure + rate × lift.

sources.title: Under Pressure: The Importance of Getting the Right Amount of Spring Pressure
sources.supports: The lb/in definition, open = installed + rate × lift, and "keep a minimum of .060 between coils".

concepts.distinctions: The spring manufacturer's specifications take precedence. Leave clearance between the coils at full lift so the spring cannot coil-bind; Engine Builder suggests at least 0.060 in for the applications it discusses, but that is a guideline for those applications, not a universal minimum for every spring.

spring_rate.note: Computes it from a load test.

caveats: "The spring manufacturer's specifications take precedence" is editorial guidance, not a sourced technical claim.

concepts.definition: The ratio of spring or damper travel to wheel travel for a given suspension movement.
concepts.distinctions: Some sources define it the other way up (wheel travel over spring travel); check which convention a calculator uses. It is also called the installation ratio; under either name, some references mean the inverse ratio. Gearhead Labs' Suspension Motion Ratio and Motion Ratio (Road Course) calculators use spring travel ÷ wheel travel.

sources.title: Spring rate in racing suspension: wheel rate, motion ratio and how to calculate what your tire actually feels
sources.author: Aaron Lambert
sources.supports: Spring ÷ wheel displacement, and "Some calculate it as wheel travel divided by spring travel."

sources.title: Motion ratio
sources.supports: The name "installation ratio", and that the term is "sometimes" used for the reciprocal.

wheel_motion.note: Uses it (its formula uses spring ÷ wheel).

caveats: "Installation ratio" is kept only with the qualification in the watch-out; "leverage ratio" and "lever ratio" are not used because no reliable source supports them as synonyms.
The calculator conventions come from the calculators' own help text: "Motion Ratio = Spring Travel ÷ Wheel Travel" and "Motion ratio = spring travel / wheel travel".

concepts.definition: The effective spring rate measured at the wheel: the spring rate multiplied by the square of the motion ratio (spring travel over wheel travel).

sources.title: Spring rate in racing suspension: wheel rate, motion ratio and how to calculate what your tire actually feels
sources.supports: Wheel rate = spring rate x motion ratio squared, with motion ratio as spring over wheel travel.

concepts.definition: The natural frequency at which a corner of the sprung mass bounces on its wheel rate, usually given in hertz or cycles per minute.

sources.title: Glossary of Suspension Terms
sources.supports: Wheel (ride) frequency = square root of wheel rate over sprung mass.

concepts.review_notes: Not confirmed in the source: the units (Hz or cycles per minute).

concepts.definition: A notional point, in a front or rear view, at which the cornering forces in the suspension are reacted into the sprung body. It is found from the suspension link geometry and moves as the suspension moves.

sources.title: Roll center
sources.supports: A notional point at which the cornering forces in the suspension are reacted to the body; found from the link geometry; it moves as the suspension moves.

sources.title: Glossary of Suspension Terms
sources.supports: Roll centre definition.

concepts.review_notes: Revised 2026-10-26: the draft described it as the point the body rolls about; the source treats it as a notional point where cornering forces are reacted, and notes that it moves.

concepts.definition: The moment needed to roll the body by one degree (or radian), from the springs and anti-roll bars of an axle.
concepts.distinctions: The front-to-rear split of roll stiffness (roll couple distribution) is a separate quantity from either axle's roll stiffness.

sources.title: Glossary of Suspension Terms
sources.supports: Roll stiffness comes from the springs and anti-roll bars and is given as torque per degree of roll.

concepts.review_notes: Not confirmed in the source: the "watch out" statement on roll couple distribution.

concepts.definition: How much of the rear load transfer under acceleration the suspension geometry carries through its links instead of the springs, given as a percentage. At 100% the rear suspension does not compress (squat) from acceleration forces.

sources.title: Anti-squat, dive and lift geometry
sources.supports: With 100% anti-squat the rear suspension does not compress from acceleration forces; anti geometry sets how much load goes through the springs.

concepts.review_notes: Revised 2026-10-26: wording aligned with the source (what 100% means).

concepts.definition: How much of the front load transfer under braking the suspension geometry carries through its links instead of the springs, given as a percentage. At 100% the front suspension does not compress (dive) from braking forces.

sources.title: Anti-squat, dive and lift geometry
sources.supports: With 100% anti-dive the front suspension does not compress from braking forces; it also depends on brake bias.

concepts.review_notes: Revised 2026-10-26: wording aligned with the source (what 100% means).

concepts.definition: The change in vertical tyre load between front and rear (under acceleration or braking) or between left and right (in a corner), caused by the centre of gravity being above the ground.
concepts.distinctions: It is load moving between tyres; the vehicle's total weight does not change.

sources.title: Weight transfer
sources.supports: Change of the load borne by the wheels under acceleration, braking or cornering, caused by the centre of mass being above the ground; the total load is redistributed, not changed.

concepts.definition: The angle of the wheels relative to the vehicle centreline seen from above: toe-in when the fronts of the tyres point towards each other, toe-out when they point apart.

sources.title: Mastering the Basics: Wheel Alignment
sources.supports: Toe-in and toe-out definitions.

sources.title: Wheel Alignment Basics Explained
sources.supports: Toe seen from above relative to the centreline.

concepts.definition: The change of toe as the suspension moves up and down, which steers the wheel without any steering input. It happens when the tie rod and the suspension links swing through different arcs, so the tie rod's effective length changes.

sources.title: Bump steer
sources.supports: The wheel steers itself (toe change) as the suspension moves, because the steering and suspension links travel on different arcs and the effective tie-rod length changes.

concepts.review_notes: Revised 2026-10-26: cause wording made specific (different arcs, effective tie-rod length).

concepts.definition: The fore-and-aft tilt of the steering axis seen from the side; positive caster tilts the top of the axis rearward.

sources.title: Mastering the Basics: Wheel Alignment
sources.supports: Caster is the fore-aft tilt of the steering axis; positive caster tilts the top rearward.

sources.title: Wheel Alignment Basics Explained
sources.supports: Caster seen from the side.

concepts.definition: The inward or outward tilt of the wheel seen from the front; negative camber tilts the top of the wheel inward, positive camber tilts it outward.

sources.title: What is Wheel Alignment? A Complete Guide
sources.supports: The definition, keeping the tread "as flat as possible on the road during turning", inner-side wear when there is too much negative camber ("too much can cause the inside of the tire to wear down quickly"), and toe affecting wear ("Toe affects the tires' directional control and wear patterns").

sources.title: Wheel Alignment Basics Explained
sources.supports: The negative and positive camber definitions.

concepts.distinctions: Camber is set to keep the tread as flat as possible on the road while cornering, for grip; excessive negative camber can contribute to inner-edge tire wear, though toe and other alignment conditions also affect wear.

concepts.definition: Steering geometry in which the inside front wheel turns more than the outside so both follow circles about a common centre.

sources.title: Ackermann steering geometry
sources.supports: The inside wheel turns more than the outside so all wheels turn about a common centre on the rear-axle line.
